where: the "≠ Changed" pill on Priya Raman's row, against "◌ Queued", "‖ Waiting" and "◷ Sending", and the "In flight 4" filter count that gathers all four
finding: Inside the new dashed family, hue is supposed to carry only severity — and it does not. Four states share one amber: three of them are jobs still running, which ask nothing of the reader, and the fourth is a job that finished on a value nobody typed and needs a decision. The filter row then states the grouping out loud: the count that gathers those four amber rows is labelled "In flight", so the screen asserts that a settled disagreement is still on its way. Scanning the list for J2's three answers — done / running / needs me — the reader sorts by colour into green, amber and red, and Priya lands in the bucket marked 'leave it alone'. She is the one row on the list that will never resolve itself, and the composition files her with the three that will.
evidence: Ava ◌ Queued, Marcus ‖ Waiting, Sofia ◷ Sending and Priya ≠ Changed are the identical warn dash, warn text, same size and weight; the markup gives all four the same tone class. The counts are In flight 4 (exactly those four) and Saves failed 1 (Benson alone). Zoe's ✓ Saved is green and Benson's ⚠ Failed is red, so the list already has a working three-way colour sort — differs is simply on the wrong side of it.
direction: Make the family's hue answer the only question a leader asks down a list of forty-five: is this mine to do something about? Running and landed need nothing; differs and failed do. Move differs out of the running colour into the needs-a-human one, and make the counts agree with the same three buckets rather than cutting them differently — one pill that gathers everything waiting on her, not one that quietly includes a state that is finished.

where: the leading glyphs across the family — ⚠ on "Failed" against ⚠ on the filled "Allergy" badge on the same row; ‖ on "Waiting" here against ‖ on "Held" in sync-outage; ◌ on "Queued" against ◌ on "No record"
finding: The dashed outline landed and does separate a job from a standing flag at a glance — but the glyph, which was meant to be the part that sorts before any word is read, is overloaded three ways. ⚠ is already the app's standing mark for allergies, so the one character that crosses the boundary the round was spent drawing is the failure mark. ‖ means 'waiting, it resumes on its own' on this screen and 'held, and no retry of yours will help' on the outage screen. ◌ means both 'queued' and 'has no upstream record at all'. Six marks were claimed and three of them are ambiguous, which leaves the word doing the work the mark was introduced to take over.
evidence: Ava's row reads ◌ Queued + ⚠ Allergy; Benson's reads ⚠ Failed + No contact — reading only the glyphs down the column gives ⚠ twice for two different families. Amara's ◌ No record is the same character as Ava's ◌ Queued in a different ink. The outage list carries nine ‖ Held pills, the same character sync-students uses for the state the brief says must never read as stuck.
direction: Spend a distinct mark on each state and do not spend one the standing badges already own — failure needs a character that is not the allergy character, and the two 'stopped' states need to be told apart by their marks and not only by their colour. If six distinct marks is more than this vocabulary can carry, cut the set: the states that ask nothing of the reader could share one mark and let colour do the rest, so the marks that are left are the ones worth learning.

where: the count discs in the quick-filter row — "Incomplete profiles 10", "In flight 4", "Saves failed 1", "Visitors 1"
finding: Four counts, three visible treatments. The neutral counts sit on a grey disc and the in-flight count on an amber one, but the danger tint at the same alpha has no luminance against the chip body, so "Saves failed" renders as a bare red digit floating after its label with no container. The one number on the row that means somebody's correction was refused is the only one that has lost its shape, and at a glance it reads as a stray mark or a superscript rather than as a count on the same footing as the others.
evidence: "10", "4" and "1 (Visitors)" each sit in a filled disc; the "1" after "Saves failed" has none, and the gap between label and numeral is consequently wider than in any other chip in the row. The same thing happens on sync-outage, where "Saves held 9" is a bare red 9 beside "Incomplete profiles 10" on its disc.
direction: The counts are one object in four instances and should read that way — the danger and warn counts need the same presence as the neutral ones, which means the alarming tone has to be lifted until its disc actually carries at this size rather than reusing the alpha that works for amber.

where: the two-up cells "YOU TYPED / Chen-Ito" and "PLANNING CENTER HOLDS / Ito" inside the amber strip
finding: The comparison is the reason this scene exists and its two halves do not line up. The right label is twice the length of the left, so it wraps, and the two values it exists to set against each other land on different baselines — the eye reads down the left cell, drops a line, and hunts for the second value. The left cell is then left with a dead band under its value while the right is full, so the pair reads as two boxes that happen to be adjacent rather than as one object with two columns.
evidence: "PLANNING CENTER HOLDS" runs to two lines while "YOU TYPED" runs to one; "Chen-Ito" sits roughly a line height above "Ito", and the bottom third of the left cell is empty. Both cells carry a neutral ink fill and ring inside a warn panel, which also gives them the silhouette of two read-only text inputs.
direction: Set the two on a shared grid so the labels occupy one band and the values another and the two values sit on one baseline — that is the whole payload of the comparison. Shorter, matched labels would do it; so would the pair reading as one framed object with a divider rather than two separate boxes.

where: the page-level danger strip, placed after the "Students / 45 students" title and the New visitor / Add from Planning Center / Export CSV stack and directly above Search
finding: A notice that governs the entire screen arrives fourth. Above it sit three routine secondary buttons that stagger diagonally down the right edge, so the first thing the frame offers is a ragged staircase of grey and the alarm is what you find underneath it. And because it butts straight onto Search and the filter block with the same gap it has to the buttons, it groups downward — it reads as a banner belonging to the filters rather than as a condition of the page. On the fold this costs everything: the strip and the filters together fill the screen and not one student row is visible.
evidence: In the fold frame the reading order is Students → New visitor → Add from Planning Center → Export CSV → the red strip. The gap above the strip and the gap below it are the same, and nothing separates it from the Search label.
direction: Put the page's condition directly under the page's name, before its routine actions, and give it more clearance below than above so it binds upward to the title rather than downward into the filters. If the actions must stay first they should at least stop staircasing, so the alarm is not queued behind three ragged rectangles.

where: the held managed fields — the values "Amara", "Whitfield", "7th grade" inside their boxes, and the six repetitions of "◌ Held until her record exists." beneath them
finding: The block says its state twice, and both registers are wrong by the same distance in opposite directions. The reason is repeated verbatim under every held field in saturated amber — four of them visible at once — so the annotations become the most colourful thing in the form and a set of fields that are merely waiting reads as a column of six rejections. Meanwhile the values themselves are dimmed to exactly the grey the app uses for placeholder text, so a name that is on file is indistinguishable from an empty box, on the one screen whose subject is what is and is not recorded about this child.
evidence: "Amara" and "Whitfield" sit at the same ink as the "Name…" placeholder on the students search field, and the empty Nickname box below them is visually the same object with the same amber sentence under it. The amber hint out-saturates every field label in the frame, and the notice at the head of the sheet has already said the same sentence at full strength.
direction: Swap the emphases. The explanation is already made once, loudly, at the head of the block — the per-field mark only has to say 'this one is in that set', so let it be the quiet member: a mark or a muted line, not the sentence repeated in the loudest colour on screen. And a held value is still a value: it needs to sit above placeholder ink so a leader can tell a filled locked field from an empty one.
